doc.title: Manny Albam interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

chapter: Longer forms, chamber music and teaching
title: Studying with Tibor Serly and writing for tuba and string quartet
summary: Frightened by Bernstein's request, he studies with Tibor Serly, and writes for Harvey Phillips' tuba and quartet.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: And it scared the hell out of me. And I started studying. I asked around and people said, “you ought to go to Tibor Serly and study.” I had never studied writing or anything. And he was Dell Barkhart’s roommate and they went to the Conservatory of Budapest together and they studied with Kodaly. Kodaly was their teacher. So I figured, yeah, why not? And he really put me into a whole different way of thinking about form, about overall form, and I’d already thought about longer works. Barnet got me to do something once that he had the faith in me that I could pull off a 15, 20 minute piece. And “The Blues is Everybody’s Business” was a result of his having that kind of faith. And I began to think about longer things, which leads me into chamber music and other things that I do besides just jazz arranging and all that. I had one experience, Harvey Phillips, I don’t know if you know Harvey.

Incredible tuba player. He calls me up and he says, “Manny, I’ve got a string quartet and me and we’re coming into Carnegie Hall. I’ve got Carnegie Hall booked but I don’t have any music.” “So what do you want me to do, Harv?” He says, “well write something.” So I wrote a four movement piece for tuba and string quartet. And people said tuba and string quartet, you’re crazy. You know, the tuba will wipe them out. It doesn’t. I figured out if you write for any one instrument against any other instruments, they’re not going to overbalance each other. There’s no problem. Okay.
